title: Tetzaveh: names over the heart (Exodus 28:12, 29)
hook: the high priest carries the tribes' names on his shoulders and over his heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, kohen, the priest, dressed for splendor and for beauty. Your line was clothes carry meaning. Today, what's written on those clothes.

Some people keep a list of names. A grandmother who prays every night through her grandchildren, one by one, oldest to youngest. A nurse who keeps the first names of patients she's lost on a folded card in her wallet. A soldier with a buddy's name on a bracelet. The high priest of Israel was asked to carry an entire people this way, on his clothes, every time he went into the sanctuary. Twice over, in two different places on his body.
screen: `A LIST OF NAMES.` → `ON PAPER, ON METAL.` → `A WHOLE PEOPLE, ON HIS CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: First, the shoulders. On the ephod, the high priest's apron, there are two shoulder straps, and on each sits an onyx stone. Engraved on the two stones, six and six, are the names of the twelve tribes of Israel, in the order they were born. The verse says Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD upon his two shoulders for a memorial. Then, the heart. Hanging in front of his chest is the breastplate, the choshen: a square of woven cloth set with twelve precious stones in four rows of three, each engraved with one tribe's name. In the old Jewish translation: "And Aaron shall bear the names of the children of Israel in the breastplate of judgment upon his heart." The same twelve names, carried in two places. Some readers have dwelt on the difference. The shoulders are where you carry weight: a burden, a responsibility. The heart is where you carry love: the people as people you care about. A leader needs both. Only shoulders, and the people become a weight. Only heart, and nothing gets carried. And one more thing. On the shoulders, two big stones hold six names each. On the heart, every tribe gets its own stone. Nobody is grouped. Each name is held one by one, and every time Aaron went in before God, he walked in wearing them all.
screen: `TWO ONYX STONES, SIX AND SIX.` · `THE CHOSHEN: TWELVE STONES.` · `SHOULDERS FOR WEIGHT, HEART FOR LOVE.` · `ON THE HEART, ONE BY ONE.` · then, large: `NAMES ON THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Let a few names come to mind, people who need carrying right now: someone sick, someone grieving, someone just starting something hard. Say each name slowly, on its own, without grouping them. If you pray, hold each one before God the way Aaron carried them; if not, let each name rest, for a breath, over your heart.
Tetzaveh. You shall command. Our portion, where the high priest carries the twelve tribes' names on his shoulders and over his heart.
Your line: names on the heart. Shoulders for weight, the heart for love. That's day three hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Jews pray for the sick by name, often in the Mi Sheberakh prayer said during the Torah reading, where people call out the names of those who need healing, and in the Amidah's blessing for healing.

chat.says: Why did the high priest wear the tribes' names twice, on his shoulders and his chest?
options: Some readers say the shoulders carry the people as weight, the heart carries them with love.
One set was for the priests' own tribe, the other for the tribes outside the sanctuary.
The shoulder stones were spares, in case a breastplate stone ever cracked.
chat.meaning: The same twelve names sit on the shoulder stones and the breastplate; some readers hear weight on the shoulders and love on the heart.
